What's happening?
The PGP key currently used to verify GitHub CLI Linux packages is expiring on Saturday, September 5, 2026. We have generated a new key and have already published an updated keyring file that contains both the old and new keys on Wednesday, April 8, 2026. This table lists the current and the new PGP key fingerprint:
Key	Fingerprint
Current key (expires September 5, 2026)	2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059
New key	7F38BBB59D064DBCB3D84D725612B36462313325
As a background, back in September 2024, our PGP signing key expired (#9569), disrupting Linux package installs and updates. At that time, we extended the expiration of the existing key as an emergency fix. This time, however, we are proactively rotating to a brand-new key well ahead of the expiry date.
Check out Am I affected? below to see if you are going to be affected by this change. For affected users, package install and update operations that rely on the old key will start failing after the expiry date unless you follow the steps outlined in this document. Scenario	Affected?

Installed gh via dnf, yum, or zypper before the new keyring was published (April 8, 2026) and haven't re-run the installation steps since	Yes. See Existing RPM users.
Installed gh using official docs after the new keyring was published (April 8, 2026)	No. Your keyring already contains the new key.

How to confirm locally installed keyring?
If you do not remember when you installed gh from the official docs, you can easily confirm if you are going to be affected by checking your local configuration. Follow the subsection that applies to you.
Debian/Ubuntu
Tip
If gpg is not installed, you can install it with:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install gnupg
Check how many keys are in your local keyring file:
gpg --show-keys /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
Tip
If the file is not found at that path, try the older location:
gpg --show-keys /usr/share/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
If you still cannot find the keyring file, check your APT source entry to see the path it references:
cat /etc/apt/sources.list.d/github-cli.list
Look for the signed-by= value in the output, which points to your keyring file path.
If the output shows two public key entries (with fingerprints 2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059 and 7F38BBB59D064DBCB3D84D725612B36462313325), you already have the updated keyring and no action is needed. This is what the output should look like:
pub   rsa4096 2022-09-06 [SC] [expires: 2026-09-05]
      2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059
uid                      GitHub CLI <opensource+cli@github.com>
sub   rsa4096 2022-09-06 [E] [expires: 2026-09-05]

pub   rsa4096 2026-04-07 [SC]
      7F38BBB59D064DBCB3D84D725612B36462313325
uid                      GitHub CLI <opensource+cli@github.com>
sub   rsa4096 2026-04-07 [E]

If only one key is listed (the old key 2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059), you need to update your keyring. See Existing APT users.
RHEL/Fedora/CentOS/openSUSE/SUSE/Amazon Linux 2
Check which GitHub CLI keys are imported in your RPM keyring:
rpm -qa gpg-pubkey | xargs -I{} sh -c 'rpm -qi {} | grep -q "opensource+cli@github.com" && echo {}'
If the output includes only one entry (the old key), you will need to update. See Existing RPM users.
If you see a second key entry, your system already has the new key and no action is needed.
What do I need to do?
New users
If you are installing gh for the first time, simply follow the standard Linux installation instructions. The current keyring file already contains the new key, so no extra steps are needed. This also applies if you installed gh for the first time after the new keyring was published (April 8, 2026).
Existing APT users (Debian/Ubuntu)
You need to replace your local copy of the keyring file. Run either of the following commands to download the updated keyring:
Using wget
sudo mkdir -p -m 755 /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo wget -qO /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg 
&& sudo chmod go+r /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
Using curl
sudo mkdir -p -m 755 /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo curl -fsSL -o /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg 
&& sudo chmod go+r /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
Then update your package lists and upgrade gh:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install gh
Note
If your keyring file is located elsewhere (e.g., under /usr/share/keyrings/), you should update that path in the command above. However, the recommended location is /etc/apt/keyrings/. Regardless of the path, make sure the signed-by field in the APT source entry (at /etc/apt/sources.list.d/github-cli.list) points at the right keyring file.
Tip
You can verify the updated keyring contains both keys by running:
gpg --show-keys /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
You should see an output like this:
pub   rsa4096 2022-09-06 [SC] [expired: 2026-09-05]
      2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059
uid                      GitHub CLI <opensource+cli@github.com>
sub   rsa4096 2022-09-06 [E] [expired: 2026-09-05]

pub   rsa4096 2026-04-07 [SC]
      7F38BBB59D064DBCB3D84D725612B36462313325
uid                      GitHub CLI <opensource+cli@github.com>
sub   rsa4096 2026-04-07 [E]

Docker build failing?
If your Docker build is failing because a layer previously added our package repository and a later layer runs apt update or apt-get update, you need to ensure the updated keyring is present.
If you control the layer that adds the keyring, rebuild it so it pulls the latest keyring file.
If you don't control that layer, add a new layer before any apt update or apt-get update that fetches the updated keyring:
RUN wget -qO /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg 
&& chmod go+r /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
Or if you prefer using curl:
RUN curl -fsSL -o /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg 
&& chmod go+r /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
If you don't use gh at all and it just happens to be in a base image, you can remove the repository so that apt update or apt-get update no longer try to verify it:
sudo rm /etc/apt/sources.list.d/github-cli.list
Existing RPM users (Fedora, RHEL, CentOS, Amazon Linux 2, openSUSE/SUSE)
RPM-based systems import PGP keys into their own keyring at install time. To pick up the new key, you need to re-fetch the repository configuration file, which now references an updated keyring. Choose the instructions matching your package manager below.
Note that when upgrading gh at the end, your package manager will prompt you to confirm importing the PGP keys. Verify that the key fingerprints match the following:

Old key: 2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059
New key: 7F38BBB59D064DBCB3D84D725612B36462313325

Important
Instructions below mimic our Linux installation guide. So, please make sure you follow the heading that you originally used to install gh.
DNF5 (Fedora 41 or newer)
Tip
Run dnf --version if you are unsure what version you are using.
Note
Ensure the config-manager plugin is installed (for example, sudo dnf install dnf5-plugins).
sudo dnf config-manager addrepo --overwrite --from-repofile=https://cli.github.com/packages/rpm/gh-cli.repo
sudo dnf update gh
DNF4 (CentOS, RHEL, Fedora 40 or earlier)
Tip
Run dnf --version if you are unsure what version you are using.
Note
Ensure the config-manager plugin is installed (for example, sudo dnf install 'dnf-command(config-manager)').
sudo dnf config-manager --add-repo https://cli.github.com/packages/rpm/gh-cli.repo
sudo dnf update gh
Yum (Amazon Linux 2)
Note
Ensure the config-manager plugin is installed (for example, sudo yum install yum-utils).
sudo yum-config-manager --add-repo https://cli.github.com/packages/rpm/gh-cli.repo
sudo yum update gh
Zypper (openSUSE/SUSE)
sudo zypper removerepo gh-cli
sudo zypper addrepo https://cli.github.com/packages/rpm/gh-cli.repo
sudo zypper update gh
Removing old key from RPM keyrings
If you still encounter key verification errors after re-adding the repository, you may need to remove the old key from the RPM keyring first:


Find the old PGP key:
sudo rpm -qa gpg-pubkey
Our old PGP key is usually named gpg-pubkey-75716059-63172e8a or gpg-pubkey-2c6106201985b60e6c7ac87323f3d4ea75716059-63172e8a. You can confirm the correct key by checking its Packager field:
sudo rpm -qi gpg-pubkey-75716059-63172e8a
or
sudo rpm -qi gpg-pubkey-2c6106201985b60e6c7ac87323f3d4ea75716059-63172e8a
The Packager should be GitHub CLI <opensource+cli@github.com>.


Once you have confirmed the Packager, remove the old PGP key:
sudo rpm -e gpg-pubkey-75716059-63172e8a
or
sudo rpm -e gpg-pubkey-2c6106201985b60e6c7ac87323f3d4ea75716059-63172e8a


Then remove and reinstall gh:
sudo dnf remove gh
sudo dnf install gh
(Replace dnf with yum or zypper as appropriate.)


Background
In September 2024, our PGP signing key expired (#9569), disrupting Linux package installs and updates. At that time, we extended the expiration of the existing key as an emergency fix.
This time, we are proactively rotating to a brand-new key well ahead of the expiry date. The updated keyring files (binary .gpg and ASCII armored .asc) already contain both the old and new keys, so anyone who has installed gh following our Linux installation instructions since April 8, 2026, is already covered.
Final notes
We apologize for any inconvenience this may cause. By announcing well in advance, we hope to give everyone enough time to update their keyring before the old key expires.
If you run into any problems, please follow up on this issue and we'll do our best to help.
Thank you for your patience and for using GitHub CLI!

How to confirm locally installed keyring?
If you do not remember when you installed gh from the official docs, you can easily confirm if you are going to be affected by checking your local configuration. Follow the subsection that applies to you.
Debian/Ubuntu
Tip
If gpg is not installed, you can install it with:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install gnupg
Check how many keys are in your local keyring file:
gpg --show-keys /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
Tip
If the file is not found at that path, try the older location:
gpg --show-keys /usr/share/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
If you still cannot find the keyring file, check your APT source entry to see the path it references:
cat /etc/apt/sources.list.d/github-cli.list
Look for the signed-by= value in the output, which points to your keyring file path.
If the output shows two public key entries (with fingerprints 2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059 and 7F38BBB59D064DBCB3D84D725612B36462313325), you already have the updated keyring and no action is needed. This is what the output should look like:
pub   rsa4096 2022-09-06 [SC] [expires: 2026-09-05]
      2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059
uid                      GitHub CLI <opensource+cli@github.com>
sub   rsa4096 2022-09-06 [E] [expires: 2026-09-05]

pub   rsa4096 2026-04-07 [SC]
      7F38BBB59D064DBCB3D84D725612B36462313325
uid                      GitHub CLI <opensource+cli@github.com>
sub   rsa4096 2026-04-07 [E]

If only one key is listed (the old key 2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059), you need to update your keyring. See Existing APT users.
RHEL/Fedora/CentOS/openSUSE/SUSE/Amazon Linux 2
Check which GitHub CLI keys are imported in your RPM keyring:
rpm -qa gpg-pubkey | xargs -I{} sh -c 'rpm -qi {} | grep -q "opensource+cli@github.com" && echo {}'
If the output includes only one entry (the old key), you will need to update. See Existing RPM users.
If you see a second key entry, your system already has the new key and no action is needed.
What do I need to do?
New users
If you are installing gh for the first time, simply follow the standard Linux installation instructions. The current keyring file already contains the new key, so no extra steps are needed. This also applies if you installed gh for the first time after the new keyring was published (April 8, 2026).
Existing APT users (Debian/Ubuntu)
You need to replace your local copy of the keyring file. Run either of the following commands to download the updated keyring:
Using wget
sudo mkdir -p -m 755 /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo wget -qO /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg 
&& sudo chmod go+r /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
Using curl
sudo mkdir -p -m 755 /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo curl -fsSL -o /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg 
&& sudo chmod go+r /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
Then update your package lists and upgrade gh:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install gh
Note
If your keyring file is located elsewhere (e.g., under /usr/share/keyrings/), you should update that path in the command above. However, the recommended location is /etc/apt/keyrings/. Regardless of the path, make sure the signed-by field in the APT source entry (at /etc/apt/sources.list.d/github-cli.list) points at the right keyring file.
Tip
You can verify the updated keyring contains both keys by running:
gpg --show-keys /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
You should see an output like this:

Docker build failing?
If your Docker build is failing because a layer previously added our package repository and a later layer runs apt update or apt-get update, you need to ensure the updated keyring is present.
If you control the layer that adds the keyring, rebuild it so it pulls the latest keyring file.
If you don't control that layer, add a new layer before any apt update or apt-get update that fetches the updated keyring:
RUN wget -qO /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg 
&& chmod go+r /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
Or if you prefer using curl:
RUN curl -fsSL -o /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg 
&& chmod go+r /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg
If you don't use gh at all and it just happens to be in a base image, you can remove the repository so that apt update or apt-get update no longer try to verify it:
sudo rm /etc/apt/sources.list.d/github-cli.list
Existing RPM users (Fedora, RHEL, CentOS, Amazon Linux 2, openSUSE/SUSE)
RPM-based systems import PGP keys into their own keyring at install time. To pick up the new key, you need to re-fetch the repository configuration file, which now references an updated keyring. Choose the instructions matching your package manager below.
Note that when upgrading gh at the end, your package manager will prompt you to confirm importing the PGP keys. Verify that the key fingerprints match the following:

Old key: 2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059
New key: 7F38BBB59D064DBCB3D84D725612B36462313325

Important
Instructions below mimic our Linux installation guide. So, please make sure you follow the heading that you originally used to install gh.
DNF5 (Fedora 41 or newer)
Tip
Run dnf --version if you are unsure what version you are using.
Note
Ensure the config-manager plugin is installed (for example, sudo dnf install dnf5-plugins).
sudo dnf config-manager addrepo --overwrite --from-repofile=https://cli.github.com/packages/rpm/gh-cli.repo
sudo dnf update gh
DNF4 (CentOS, RHEL, Fedora 40 or earlier)
Tip
Run dnf --version if you are unsure what version you are using.
Note
Ensure the config-manager plugin is installed (for example, sudo dnf install 'dnf-command(config-manager)').
sudo dnf config-manager --add-repo https://cli.github.com/packages/rpm/gh-cli.repo
sudo dnf update gh
Yum (Amazon Linux 2)
Note
Ensure the config-manager plugin is installed (for example, sudo yum install yum-utils).
sudo yum-config-manager --add-repo https://cli.github.com/packages/rpm/gh-cli.repo
sudo yum update gh
Zypper (openSUSE/SUSE)
sudo zypper removerepo gh-cli
sudo zypper addrepo https://cli.github.com/packages/rpm/gh-cli.repo
sudo zypper update gh
Removing old key from RPM keyrings
If you still encounter key verification errors after re-adding the repository, you may need to remove the old key from the RPM keyring first:


Find the old PGP key:
sudo rpm -qa gpg-pubkey
Our old PGP key is usually named gpg-pubkey-75716059-63172e8a or gpg-pubkey-2c6106201985b60e6c7ac87323f3d4ea75716059-63172e8a. You can confirm the correct key by checking its Packager field:
sudo rpm -qi gpg-pubkey-75716059-63172e8a
or
sudo rpm -qi gpg-pubkey-2c6106201985b60e6c7ac87323f3d4ea75716059-63172e8a
The Packager should be GitHub CLI <opensource+cli@github.com>.


Once you have confirmed the Packager, remove the old PGP key:
sudo rpm -e gpg-pubkey-75716059-63172e8a
or
sudo rpm -e gpg-pubkey-2c6106201985b60e6c7ac87323f3d4ea75716059-63172e8a


Then remove and reinstall gh:
sudo dnf remove gh
sudo dnf install gh
(Replace dnf with yum or zypper as appropriate.)

You're right, @joshkoehler. The recommended repository file does not explicitly disable metadata signature verification. It leaves that decision to the user's DNF configuration, which is the appropriate behavior. My earlier statement that the file disables this verification was incorrect.
I was able to reproduce the failure on Fedora 32 with DNF4 and a global repo_gpgcheck=1 setting. The same test succeeded with DNF5 on Fedora 43, so the behavior differs between DNF versions.
Since we already sign our repository metadata, we should not override a user's global verification policy in gh-cli.repo. The current metadata was signed with the old key before it expired. This will be resolved with the next release, when the repository metadata is regenerated and signed with the new key.

We want package installation and update processes to remain as smooth as possible, with minimal interruption for our users. Displaying verification statuses for all of your commits
You can enable vigilant mode for commit signature verification to mark all of your commits and tags with a signature verification status.
About vigilant mode
When you work locally on your computer, Git allows you to set the author of your changes and the identity of the committer. This, potentially, makes it difficult for other people to be confident that commits and tags you create were actually created by you. To help solve this problem you can sign your commits and tags. For more information, see Signing commits and Signing tags. GitHub marks signed commits and tags with a verification status.
By default commits and tags are marked "Verified" if they are signed with a GPG, SSH, or S/MIME key that was successfully verified. If a commit or tag has a signature that can't be verified by GitHub, we mark the commit or tag "Unverified." In all other cases no verification status is displayed.
However, you can give other users increased confidence in the identity attributed to your commits and tags by enabling vigilant mode in your GitHub settings. With vigilant mode enabled, all of your commits and tags are marked with one of three verification statuses:



Status
Description




Verified
The commit is signed, the signature was successfully verified, and the committer is the only author who has enabled vigilant mode.


Partially verified
The commit is signed, and the signature was successfully verified, but the commit has an author who: a) is not the committer and b) has enabled vigilant mode. In this case, the commit signature doesn't guarantee the consent of the author, so the commit is only partially verified.


Unverified
Any of the following is true:- The commit is signed but the signature could not be verified.- The commit is not signed and the committer has enabled vigilant mode.- The commit is not signed and an author has enabled vigilant mode.



You should only enable vigilant mode if you sign all of your commits and tags and use an email address that is verified for your GitHub account as your committer email address. After enabling this mode, any unsigned commits or tags that you generate locally and push to GitHub will be marked "Unverified."
You can check the verification status of your signed commits or tags on GitHub and view why your commit signatures might be unverified. For more information, see Checking your commit and tag signature verification status.
Enabling vigilant mode

In the upper-right corner of any page on GitHub, click your profile picture, then click  Settings.
In the "Access" section of the sidebar, click  SSH and GPG keys.
Under "Vigilant mode," select Flag unsigned commits as unverified.

Debian/Ubuntu
Tip

If you still encounter key verification errors after re-adding the repository, you may need to remove the old key from the RPM keyring first:
1. Find the old PGP key:
   sudo rpm -qa gpg-pubkey

   sudo rpm -qi gpg-pubkey-75716059-63172e8a
   # or
   sudo rpm -qi gpg-pubkey-2c6106201985b60e6c7ac87323f3d4ea75716059-63172e8a

2. Once you have confirmed the Packager, remove the old PGP key:
   sudo rpm -e gpg-pubkey-75716059-63172e8a
   # or
   sudo rpm -e gpg-pubkey-2c6106201985b60e6c7ac87323f3d4ea75716059-63172e8a

3. Then remove and reinstall `gh`:
   sudo dnf remove gh
   sudo dnf install gh
       
         
       
   
         
       
   
       
     
   (Replace `dnf` with `yum` or `zypper` as appropriate.)

nodes.title: `gh auth login` freezes after selecting `Github.com` on Ubuntu 20.04

nodes.bodyText: Thanks for reporting. Could you check if this matches your scenario? #7208 (comment)

That helped me: #7145 (comment)
@mislav thank you! 🙇
I followed the linux install instructions and it's still hanging indefinitely for me. Running WSL2 (Ubuntu) and gh auth login is hanging ~15 minutes then crashing

@RobertGemmaJr This looks like a problem with opening your web browser. Command line tools usually invoke the tool xdg-open <URL> to open a URL in your web browser. However, for that to work, a web browser needs to be set up on the system. Please check that it works, and install a browser if it doesn't. You can also set the GH_BROWSER environment variable to point to another command-line tool that will be used to open a graphical browser.

This failed for me from within tmux. Opening a shell outside of tmux allowed things to work properly. Perhaps someone could weigh in on what in my tmux environment isn't configured correctly to cause this to happen?
Subsequent commands in tmux are also failing.

When I select Github.com from gh auth login, it freezes for me, If I select the enterprise option, It works
Currently, I am using Linux 6.1.31-2-MANJARO [x86_64]
It used to freeze with Archlinux too,
The -w tag doesn't work either,  In case it matters, I use i3wm but have tried with GNOME (on Arch) too and have reproduced the same bug.
The reason in my case that this wasn't working is that I didn't have the DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS envar set from within tmux.
I have reproduced the issue outside of tmux. I have even tried this on different shells (bash, fish, zsh) and terminal emulators (alacritty, kitty) but it freezes everywhere.
@abbas-pullflow Can you confirm you have the DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS envar set?

I invoked the gh auth login command, observed same behaviour, waited for several minutes and it gave me the expected response (i-e asking for HTTPS). Perhaps it is just taking too long and isn't getting frozen.

DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS was already set to unix:path=/tmp/dbus-cXvBcLdNjA,guid=3779f31ea57565b018de466764a5d1ef and I didn't reset it.
Still happening to me...

nodes.title: `gh pr checks` exits 1 for "no checks reported", the same code as failed checks

nodes.bodyText:
Thanks for the detailed report and investigation. I verified the current source: populateStatusChecks in pkg/cmd/pr/checks/checks.go#L303 returns a plain fmt.Errorf("no checks reported on the '%s' branch", ...) when the status check rollup is empty, which propagates as a generic error and exits 1 — the same as counts.Failed > 0 returning cmdutil.SilentError. By contrast, the pending case at L250-251 uses the documented cmdutil.PendingError, mapped to exit code 8, and the help text's "Additional exit codes" section (L73-74) only documents that one. So the hypothesis — that "no checks" and "checks failed" are indistinguishable by exit code because the former isn't routed through a distinct sentinel error — matches the code. I didn't find an exact duplicate; a related issue (#9682) asked for a similar distinction but only for the --required variant and its linked fix was closed without merging. I'm suggesting bug, priority-3 (a workaround exists via message-matching or gh pr view --json statusCheckRollup), and gh-pr for the affected command.

nodes.title: gh release list получает Forbidden при POS

nodes.bodyText:
Thanks for the report. I searched existing issues and didn't find an exact duplicate of a Forbidden response from gh release list against api.github.com/graphql.
However, the report is missing information needed to investigate: the output of gh version, the full/exact error text printed by the command, and clear reproduction steps (which repository, what command was run, and whether the token/account has access to that repo). A 403 Forbidden on the GraphQL endpoint is commonly caused by a corporate proxy/firewall blocking or modifying requests to api.github.com, or by insufficient token scopes for the target repository — not necessarily a gh bug — but we can't confirm which without more detail.
I'm suggesting more-info-needed so a maintainer can ask for these specifics, and gh-release since this concerns the gh release list command. No priority is suggested given the current information gap.

nodes.bodyText: Any plans to work on this issue? A month later it's still a problem.

@ryan-williams, @kperkins-godaddy, @andykingit, @richmondjerry, @dlvhdr, @ptorgalmath-gpsw we're implementing a fallback approach (stated in #11118 and #11169, and implemented in #11172) for when gh couldn't find the logs in the downloaded ZIP archive. It's not a replacement for this issue, of course, but will fix the use cases. You're welcome to build gh from the PR's branch and test it on your end.
Hey @babakks, I just confirmed, PR #11172 works great! I can fetch all jobs' logs.

Still reproducible on gh version 2.103.3 (2026-10-26).
Since the API fallback (#11172), logs are now printed, but for any reusable-workflow job (named <caller> / <callee>) every line is labelled UNKNOWN STEP, because the step files in the ZIP are never matched.
Example: job deploy / scan (env: prod) is stored in the ZIP as deploy _ scan (env prod)/5_<step name>.txt, but getJobNameForLogFilename in pkg/cmd/run/view/logs.go deletes the / and searches for deploy  scan (env prod) (double space), so neither the job file nor any step file matches.
Replacing / with _ instead of deleting it (in getJobNameForLogFilename) matches the step files in the ZIP for our runs, so --log-failed would show real step names again.

Another data point, from a private repository, so no runs I can link. This one has no / in the job name, and the output is partial rather than empty.
gh version 2.103.2 (2026-10-23) on Linux. Two pull_request runs of the same workflow in the same repository, both attempt 1, an hour apart, each with one job named Build, typecheck, test (npm):

Run 1. The archive from GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/{id}/logs holds only Build, typecheck, test (npm)/system.txt and the top-level 0_Build, typecheck, test (npm).txt (242,885 bytes). gh run view <id> --log prints the whole job, 1601 lines.
Run 2. The archive holds the same top-level 0_…txt (242,978 bytes) plus per-step files: 1_Set up job.txt, 2_Run actions_checkout@v7.txt, 3_Run actions_setup-node@v7.txt, 4_Run npm ci.txt, 5_Run npm run build.txt, 6_Run npm run typecheck.txt, 7_…, 8_…, 9_…, 10_Run npm test.txt (221,105 bytes), then 18_… to 21_Complete job.txt. The jobs API lists steps 1–10 and 18–21, all success. gh run view <id> --log prints 89 lines covering steps 1, 3, 4 and 5 only, and exits 0. Step 2 is dropped, and so is everything from step 6 on, the 221 KB step 10 included. Re-running the command gives the same output.

GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/jobs/{job_id}/logs returns the complete log for run 2's job. Through gh api that needs --allow-escape-sequences, because the log contains ANSI colour codes.
So the per-step layout is not all-or-nothing: some step files are matched and others silently skipped, while the exit status stays 0. For tooling that parses --log output (we read test counts from it), that is worse than an empty result, since nothing signals that the log is incomplete. In both layouts the top-level 0_<job>.txt held the full log, which may be the more reliable source when it is present.

nodes.title: gh run view --job --log-failed fails on required shared-workflow metadata 404

nodes.bodyText:
Thanks for the detailed repro. I traced this through the source and the cause looks clear: shared.GetRun (shared.go lines 559–592 at commit 4f2cfe9) always calls workflowShared.GetWorkflow(client, repo, result.WorkflowID) right after fetching the run, and returns any error from that call unmodified. For a run whose workflow originates from an organization/enterprise ruleset rather than the consumer repo's own workflow list, that lookup 404s, so GetRun fails before view.go's --log/--log-failed path ever reaches getRunLog/job-log fetching — even though the run and job metadata and logs are otherwise readable. This matches a known pattern already handled more leniently elsewhere: preloadWorkflowNames (shared.go lines ~487–505) explicitly catches a 404 from the same GetWorkflow call for run list and falls back to an empty workflow name instead of failing, but GetRun (used by run view) has no equivalent fallback. I'm suggesting bug, gh-run, and priority-3 (narrow case with a viable gh api workaround) for maintainer review. This is not a duplicate of #9228 (which is about run list/run view generally 404ing on ruleset workflows); this issue is specifically about --log-failed/--log failing even though job logs themselves are fetchable, so a first responder may want to consider making GetRun's workflow-name lookup tolerate a 404 the same way preloadWorkflowNames does.

Generated by Issue Triage (skills-driven) for #14822 · copilot · auto · 79 AIC · ⊞ 4.5K · ◷

Analysis & Proposed Fix
In pkg/cmd/run/shared/shared.go, GetRun always calls workflowShared.GetWorkflow(client, repo, result.WorkflowID) after fetching the run and returns any error from that lookup directly:
workflow, err := workflowShared.GetWorkflow(client, repo, result.WorkflowID)
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
} else {
    result.workflowName = workflow.Name
}
When a workflow run originates from an organization or enterprise ruleset rather than a workflow file in the consumer repository, GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow_id} returns 404 Not Found even though the run metadata and job logs are readable in the consumer repository. Consequently, gh run view RUN --job JOB --log-failed fails in GetRun before reaching getRunLog.
Notably, preloadWorkflowNames in the same file (pkg/cmd/run/shared/shared.go:460-474) already handles this exact ruleset-workflow case for gh run list by catching api.HTTPError with status 404 and falling back to an empty workflow name.
Proposed Changes

pkg/cmd/run/shared/shared.go (GetRun):

Check var httpErr api.HTTPError when workflowShared.GetWorkflow returns an error; if errors.As(err, &httpErr) && httpErr.StatusCode == http.StatusNotFound, fall back to an empty workflowName instead of failing GetRun.


Tests:

Added TestGetRunWorkflow404 in pkg/cmd/run/shared/shared_test.go.
Added noninteractive with job log-failed when workflow metadata returns 404 (#14822) in pkg/cmd/run/view/view_test.go.



I have verified this fix with go test ./pkg/cmd/run/... on my fork (duongynhi000005-oss/cli-2:fix/run-view-workflow-404, commit 1f1cb05) and would be happy to open a PR if you'd like to assign this issue to me.

Additional reproduction on gh 2.103.1 (macOS), while diagnosing a required shared validate workflow for a merge-group candidate: gh run view RUN --log-failed also fails on the consumer repository's workflow-metadata endpoint with HTTP 404. The same authenticated gh api .../actions/jobs/JOB/logs --allow-escape-sequences successfully retrieved the job log to a file. This occurs for validation as well as the review-gate case above; no separate issue filed.

Additional reproduction on the same environment: gh run view RUN --repo ORG/CONSUMER --json jobs also fails at the shared required workflow metadata lookup with HTTP 404 while the run is in progress. With the same authentication, gh api repos/ORG/CONSUMER/actions/runs/RUN/jobs succeeds and returns current job states. This is therefore not limited to completed runs or log requests. No private repository/run identifiers are included here.

nodes.title: Refactor git graph tests to use real repositories

nodes.bodyText:
💭 Commentary: Preserve coverage of forced branch deletion
The feature branch points to the same commit as trunk, so this test also passes if DeleteLocalBranch is changed from forced deletion to ordinary deletion. The removed test explicitly checked the force flag, which matters when closing an unmerged PR or cleaning up after a squash merge. Create a feature-only commit and switch back to trunk before deleting the branch so the real-repository test preserves that regression coverage.

🛑 Requirement: Remove the unsupported cherry-pick option
Git cherry-pick does not support --quiet, so this setup command exits with a usage error. The run helper immediately fails the test, preventing it from reaching the Commits assertions. Remove --quiet; the helper already captures command output.

🛑 Requirement: Use a fatal assertion for the filesystem error check
The testing guide at docs/testing.md:55-57 requires error checks to use require rather than assert. Use require.ErrorIs here so an unexpected filesystem result stops the scenario before the subsequent worktree assertions.

nodes.bodyText:
🛑 Requirement: Inspect the expected error, not the actual error
This branch currently extracts GitError from err, then compares that same actual error to itself, so incorrect exit codes or stderr can pass unnoticed. Extract from tt.wantError so the assertions validate the result against the fixture.

🛑 Requirement: Cover both non-spam exception branches in the evaluator
This criterion requires same-author reposts and cross-author quotations with author-supplied context to remain legitimate. The corpus's only <AUTHOR> case covers the spam branch; existing PASS cases omit <AUTHOR>, so they cannot verify either the author comparison or the context exception once the repost is known to be cross-author. Add explicit PASS fixtures for both cases to prevent legitimate issues from being auto-closed by a future prompt change.
